lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter Six · New Jersey|Mahlon Dickerson · Princeton, class of 1789

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Washington, 1834. A former governor of New Jersey arrives in the capital ready to sail for Russia. Andrew Jackson has named him minister to the court of the czar.
lines.caption: Washington, 1834. A former governor of New Jersey arrives in the capital ready to sail for Russia. Andrew Jackson has named him minister to the court of the czar.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: When he gets to town, he learns he's not going anywhere. He's been made Secretary of the Navy instead.
lines.caption: When he gets to town, he learns he's not going anywhere. He's been made Secretary of the Navy instead.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|Named minister to Russia, he arrived to find he'd been made Secretary of the Navy

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Tigers, the party's in Jadwin. And honestly? Showing up for one job and getting another. That's just networking.
lines.caption: Tigers, the party's in Jadwin. And honestly? Showing up for one job and getting another. That's just networking.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: I showed up for a job interview once and they gave me a different job. It was worse.
lines.caption: I showed up for a job interview once and they gave me a different job. It was worse.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's how power worked when you knew the right people. Meet Mahlon Dickerson. New Jersey's seventh governor.
lines.caption: That's how power worked when you knew the right people. Meet Mahlon Dickerson. New Jersey's seventh governor.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Mahlon Dickerson was born April 17th, 1770, at Hanover Neck, New Jersey. He graduated from the College of New Jersey in 1789. Today we call it Princeton.
lines.caption: Mahlon Dickerson was born April 17th, 1770, at Hanover Neck, New Jersey. He graduated from the College of New Jersey in 1789. Today we call it Princeton.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|Princeton, then the College of New Jersey, class of 1789

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Princeton has done its own homework on that era. Its Princeton and Slavery project found that the college's first nine presidents all enslaved people at some point in their lives, and that on at least one occasion, enslaved people were auctioned at the President's House.
lines.caption: Princeton has done its own homework on that era. Its Princeton and Slavery project found that the college's first nine presidents all enslaved people at some point in their lives, and that on at least one occasion, enslaved people were auctioned at the President's House.

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Stay striped. But that's a stripe the old catalogs left out. Good on the place for printing it now.
lines.caption: Stay striped. But that's a stripe the old catalogs left out. Good on the place for printing it now.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1794 Dickerson rode as a private in the New Jersey militia cavalry, part of the army sent to put down the Whiskey Rebellion, a revolt over a federal tax on whiskey in western Pennsylvania.
lines.caption: In 1794 Dickerson rode as a private in the New Jersey militia cavalry, part of the army sent to put down the Whiskey Rebellion, a revolt over a federal tax on whiskey in western Pennsylvania.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|In 1794 he rode with the militia sent against the Whiskey Rebellion

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then he crossed into Pennsylvania government himself. He served as the state's Adjutant General, and in 1808, briefly, as its Attorney General.
lines.caption: Then he crossed into Pennsylvania government himself. He served as the state's Adjutant General, and in 1808, briefly, as its Attorney General.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: A New Jersey guy running Pennsylvania's army. That's like a Toledo guy coaching Bowling Green.
lines.caption: A New Jersey guy running Pennsylvania's army. That's like a Toledo guy coaching Bowling Green.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The count in New Jersey is the cleanest of all seven. The state counts each person once and traditionally numbered only elected governors. Acting governors who filled gaps, like John Lambert in 1802, are left off.
lines.caption: The count in New Jersey is the cleanest of all seven. The state counts each person once and traditionally numbered only elected governors. Acting governors who filled gaps, like John Lambert in 1802, are left off.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: William Livingston, William Paterson, Richard Howell, Joseph Bloomfield, Aaron Ogden, William Pennington. And number seven, Mahlon Dickerson, sworn in October 26th, 1815.
lines.caption: William Livingston, William Paterson, Richard Howell, Joseph Bloomfield, Aaron Ogden, William Pennington. And number seven, Mahlon Dickerson, sworn in October 26th, 1815.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|New Jersey counts elected governors once each · Dickerson is No. 7

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: No recounts, no asterisks. Very Princeton. We like a tidy guest list.
lines.caption: No recounts, no asterisks. Very Princeton. We like a tidy guest list.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He didn't stay long. In February 1817 he resigned the governorship to go to the United States Senate, where he served for sixteen years and chaired the committee on manufactures.
lines.caption: He didn't stay long. In February 1817 he resigned the governorship to go to the United States Senate, where he served for sixteen years and chaired the committee on manufactures.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|He resigned as governor in 1817 to go to the U.S. Senate

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then came the Navy. He ran it from 1834 to 1838, and when Martin Van Buren took over, Van Buren kept him. He sat in Jackson's cabinet in the years when the federal government was driving Native nations out of the Southeast.
lines.caption: Then came the Navy. He ran it from 1834 to 1838, and when Martin Van Buren took over, Van Buren kept him. He sat in Jackson's cabinet in the years when the federal government was driving Native nations out of the Southeast.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1840 Van Buren made him a federal judge in New Jersey. He resigned the next year, and the judgeship went to his brother, Philemon.
lines.caption: In 1840 Van Buren made him a federal judge in New Jersey. He resigned the next year, and the judgeship went to his brother, Philemon.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: He handed his judgeship to his brother?
lines.caption: He handed his judgeship to his brother?

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Gary. It's called keeping it in the family. The Griswolds did it with a governorship.
lines.caption: Gary. It's called keeping it in the family. The Griswolds did it with a governorship.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: His Senate career had one strange twist. On January 30th, 1829, Dickerson resigned his seat, and the legislature immediately elected him again, to fill a different vacancy left by another senator's resignation. Same man, same chamber, new seat.
lines.caption: His Senate career had one strange twist. On January 30th, 1829, Dickerson resigned his seat, and the legislature immediately elected him again, to fill a different vacancy left by another senator's resignation. Same man, same chamber, new seat.
lines.visual: card:January 30, 1829|Dickerson resigns his Senate seat and is re-elected the same day to another

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: He quit and got rehired before lunch.
lines.caption: He quit and got rehired before lunch.

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Gary, that's not quitting. That's a lateral move.
lines.caption: Gary, that's not quitting. That's a lateral move.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1807, the club Benjamin Franklin founded. In 1833 he was admitted to the Society of the Cincinnati, the hereditary club of Revolutionary officers and their descendants. In 1844 he helped write New Jersey's new constitution.
lines.caption: He was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1807, the club Benjamin Franklin founded. In 1833 he was admitted to the Society of the Cincinnati, the hereditary club of Revolutionary officers and their descendants. In 1844 he helped write New Jersey's new constitution.
lines.visual: card:Mahlon Dickerson|American Philosophical Society, 1807 · Society of the Cincinnati, 1833

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Clubs, clubs, clubs. Now that's a resume I respect.
lines.caption: Clubs, clubs, clubs. Now that's a resume I respect.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And while he was gathering clubs, the Navy he ran was a hard place for the men at the bottom. Sailors could still be flogged. Congress didn't ban the lash on American ships until 1850. The men at the top of the Navy didn't feel it. The men at the bottom did.
lines.caption: And while he was gathering clubs, the Navy he ran was a hard place for the men at the bottom. Sailors could still be flogged. Congress didn't ban the lash on American ships until 1850. The men at the top of the Navy didn't feel it. The men at the bottom did.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: But the real Dickerson fortune came out of the ground. From 1810 until he died, he ran mines and an ironworks in Morris County, in the hills around Succasunna.
lines.caption: But the real Dickerson fortune came out of the ground. From 1810 until he died, he ran mines and an ironworks in Morris County, in the hills around Succasunna.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|Iron mines and an ironworks in Morris County, 1810 to 1853

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Iron mining in that era was hard, dangerous work. The records we found tell us a lot about Mahlon Dickerson, his offices, his elections, his honors. They don't tell us the names of the men who went down into his mines.
lines.caption: Iron mining in that era was hard, dangerous work. The records we found tell us a lot about Mahlon Dickerson, his offices, his elections, his honors. They don't tell us the names of the men who went down into his mines.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's who gets left out of these stories. Not the governor. The miners.
lines.caption: That's who gets left out of these stories. Not the governor. The miners.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Mahlon Dickerson died in Succasunna on October 5th, 1853. Today the Mahlon Dickerson Reservation, more than three thousand acres of Morris County park land, carries his name.
lines.caption: Mahlon Dickerson died in Succasunna on October 5th, 1853. Today the Mahlon Dickerson Reservation, more than three thousand acres of Morris County park land, carries his name.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|The 3,200-acre Mahlon Dickerson Reservation is named for him

lines.speaker: PR
lines.say: Van Doren out. And Gary, take a hike there sometime. Lovely trails.
lines.caption: Van Doren out. And Gary, take a hike there sometime. Lovely trails.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: His name is on three thousand two hundred acres. Somebody ought to find the names of the people who worked them.
lines.caption: His name is on three thousand two hundred acres. Somebody ought to find the names of the people who worked them.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: So, New Jersey. Your lucky seven, one more time.
lines.caption: So, New Jersey. Your lucky seven, one more time.
